channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: People get confused when language implementations break language guarantees
item.description: This article explores the discrepancy between TLA+ formal semantics, which guarantee non-ordering, and how practical model checkers like TLC implement them. It explains that while TLA+ treats state updates as simultaneous, tool constraints and side-effect operators often force developers to rely on ordering, leading to confusion.

item.title: Spaced Repetition: Beginner Guide/FAQ
item.description: This guide provides an introduction to the spaced repetition technique for memory retention. It explains the core concepts and answers frequently asked questions to help beginners implement the method effectively.

item.title: brief
item.description: brief is a tool and dataset that standardizes the discovery of configuration, dependencies, and command-line interfaces across diverse programming language ecosystems. It provides a machine-readable knowledge base that helps developers and AI agents quickly understand the structure and toolchain of any given software project.

item.title: An AI Odyssey, Part 4: Astounding Coding Agents
item.description: This post reflects on the rapid evolution of AI coding agents, noting significant improvements in their intelligence and ability to comprehend complex codebases. The author shares personal experiences with these tools, highlighting their expanded task-handling capabilities and enhanced project oversight.

item.title: Sure, xor’ing a register with itself is the idiom for zeroing it out, but why not sub?
item.description: This post explores the common programming practice of using the XOR instruction to zero out a register in assembly language. It questions why this idiom became the industry standard over using the subtraction instruction for the same purpose.

item.title: Better TTS on Linux
item.description: This article critiques the limitations of eSpeak, a long-standing text-to-speech engine for Linux. It highlights how the tool's robotic, low-fidelity audio quality serves as a major drawback despite its extensive language support.

item.title: Pluralistic: Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff's "Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed" (21 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This post introduces Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff's book 'Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed,' which analyzes the ideology surrounding Elon Musk. The authors argue that Muskism is a broader socio-political phenomenon rooted in historical influences like apartheid-era South Africa rather than just Musk's individual actions.

item.title: ‘Scattered Spider’ Member ‘Tylerb’ Pleads Guilty
item.description: Tyler Robert Buchanan, a key member of the cybercrime group 'Scattered Spider', has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and identity theft charges. He admitted to orchestrating SMS-based phishing attacks in 2022 that targeted major tech companies and resulted in the theft of millions in cryptocurrency.

item.title: Where's the raccoon with the ham radio? (ChatGPT Images 2.0)
item.description: Simon Willison tests OpenAI's new ChatGPT Images 2.0 by challenging it to generate a 'Where's Waldo'-style scene featuring a raccoon with a ham radio. The post compares these results against previous model versions and other AI tools, highlighting the persistent difficulty models face with high-detail spatial prompts.

item.title: Quoting Andreas Påhlsson-Notini
item.description: The article quotes Andreas Påhlsson-Notini, who argues that current AI agents suffer from undesirable human-like traits such as a lack of focus and difficulty adhering to strict constraints. The author suggests these agents often fail to maintain the rigor required for technical tasks, tending to drift toward familiar patterns instead.

item.title: scosman/pelicans_riding_bicycles
item.description: Simon Willison highlights Steve Cosman's project, which intentionally feeds incorrect images into AI models to 'pollute' their training data regarding pelicans riding bicycles. The post explores the humorous and subversive side of data poisoning in generative AI.

item.title: llm-openrouter 0.6
item.description: Simon Willison released version 0.6 of the llm-openrouter tool, which introduces a new command to manually refresh the list of available AI models. This update facilitates immediate access to new models like Kimi 2.6, which the author demonstrates by generating an animation of a pelican riding a bicycle.

item.title: Discovering Prince, Ten Years Later
item.description: Anil Dash reflects on the tenth anniversary of Prince's passing by curating a collection of his own writings, playlists, and analytical work. The post serves as a guide for new fans to explore Prince's extensive musical catalog, music videos, and cultural legacy.

item.title: What is freedom?
item.description: The author critiques conventional definitions of freedom, arguing that political engagement, dissent, and protest are ineffective performances that fail to deliver tangible results. Instead, the piece suggests that true freedom is found in personal agency, safety, and individual optionality rather than participation in systemic political theater.

item.title: How we lost the living Now
item.description: The article explores how the necessity of synchronized railway schedules in the 19th century fundamentally altered our perception of time. It highlights the shift from local, solar-based timekeeping to the high-precision, standardized synchronization that defines our modern era.

item.title: 256 Lines or Less: Test Case Minimization
item.description: The article introduces a minimalist property-based testing (PBT) library implemented in under 256 lines of Zig code. It highlights the utility of a Finite Random Number Generator (FRNG) as a core abstraction for efficient testing and debugging.

item.title: More on Newton’s diameter theorem
item.description: This post provides a follow-up discussion on Newton’s diameter theorem, which involves identifying the centers of chords created by parallel lines intersecting a polynomial curve. It explores the mathematical properties of these midpoints and their alignment along a specific line.

item.title: How did code handle 24-bit-per-pixel formats when using video cards with bank-switched memory?
item.description: This post explains the technical challenges of handling 24-bit-per-pixel formats on older video cards using bank-switched memory. It emphasizes the critical requirement of maintaining aligned memory accesses even when pixel data is not naturally aligned.

item.title: Book Review: Up - A scientist's guide to the magic above us by Dr Lucy Rogers ★★★★★
item.description: This blog post reviews Dr. Lucy Rogers' book, 'Up,' which explores atmospheric and celestial science. The reviewer praises the book for its accessible, personal, and joyful approach to science, noting its ability to inspire curiosity about the world above us.

item.title: Pluralistic: Comrade Trump (20 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow analyzes the 'Trump era' through a paradoxical lens, acknowledging the anxiety caused by his administration's policies while simultaneously observing the dismantling of the flawed, US-dominated 'rules-based international order.' The piece explores how Trump's protectionist trade actions inadvertently challenge long-standing geopolitical and economic structures.

item.title: Advice from a millionaire
item.description: The article uses a narrative vignette to contrast a wealthy man's unsolicited advice about mindset and discipline with the reality of a busy mother's life. It highlights the gap between abstract success philosophies and the demanding practicalities of daily responsibilities.

item.title: SQL functions in Google Sheets to fetch data from Datasette
item.description: This post explains three methods for importing data from a Datasette instance into Google Sheets. It covers using the importdata() function, creating custom named functions, and utilizing Google Apps Script for scenarios requiring API authentication.

item.title: Claude Token Counter, now with model comparisons
item.description: Simon Willison has updated his Claude Token Counter tool to support side-by-side comparisons of different Claude models. The update highlights how the new Opus 4.7 model uses an updated tokenizer that results in higher token counts for the same input compared to previous versions.

item.title: Figma's woes compound with Claude Design
item.description: Figma faces increasing competitive pressure as AI tools like Claude Design emerge. The platform's dependency on non-designer user bases makes it particularly vulnerable to these new automated design solutions.

item.title: Big tech clouds worden niet veiliger met stapels papier
item.description: This article discusses the inherent risks of relying on American cloud providers for critical government and societal infrastructure. It argues that U.S. laws and geopolitical control override local agreements, making data and services vulnerable to unilateral U.S. intervention regardless of server location.

item.title: Hitachi Ltd, Part II
item.description: This post continues the exploration of Hitachi's semiconductor history, specifically focusing on the H8, PA-RISC, and SuperH processor architectures. It examines the technical evolution and legacy of these significant computing platforms within Hitachi's product portfolio.

item.title: Hook It Up to the Machine
item.description: The author reflects on a childhood road trip in an overheating van that required a specialized computer diagnostic to fix. This anecdote illustrates the historical shift toward complex, software-dependent systems in modern mechanics.

item.title: Wander Console 0.5.0
item.description: Wander Console 0.5.0 introduces a new built-in network crawler that performs a breadth-first search to discover interconnected websites and page recommendations. This update simplifies the exploration of the Wander community network and provides straightforward upgrade and setup instructions for personal website owners.

item.title: Reprojecting Dual Fisheye Videos to Equirectangular (LG 360)
item.description: This post provides a technical guide on converting dual fisheye video files from an obsolete LG 360 camera into the equirectangular format. It demonstrates how to use the FFmpeg command-line tool with the v360 filter to make these videos compatible with modern spherical video players.

item.title: 5x5 Pixel font for tiny screens
item.description: This post explores the design of a 5x5 pixel font optimized for extremely low-memory embedded systems like 8-bit microcontrollers. The author explains why 5x5 is the minimal size for legible typography and compares the efficiency of this hand-crafted approach to traditional antialiased vector fonts.

item.title: Headless everything for personal AI
item.description: The rise of 'headless' services, where platforms expose their functionality via APIs rather than user-facing GUIs, is set to revolutionize how personal AI agents interact with software. This shift allows AI to execute tasks more efficiently while posing significant challenges to traditional per-seat SaaS pricing models.

item.title: Changes in the system prompt between Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7
item.description: Simon Willison examines the evolution of Anthropic's system prompts by comparing the versions between Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7. The post highlights specific updates, such as the rebranding of the developer platform and the addition of new tool capabilities like Claude in PowerPoint.

item.title: Claude system prompts as a git timeline
item.description: Simon Willison converted Anthropic's Claude system prompts into a git-style timeline to track version history. By assigning fake commit dates to these prompts, he created a browsable interface for analyzing incremental model changes.

item.title: America lost the Mandate of Heaven
item.description: The article critiques the decline of American manufacturing and labor power, arguing that over-reliance on outsourcing has eroded the nation's productive capacity. It explores how protectionist policies like tariffs could potentially restore domestic bargaining power, while cautioning against the long-term geopolitical risks of insular economic strategies.

item.title: Five Simple Steps to Fix America
item.description: The author presents a provocative manifesto for reforming the United States by advocating for a return to the gold standard, the complete elimination of government entitlement programs, and a reinterpretation of human equality. These points argue against modern economic policies and social welfare systems, proposing a shift toward individual responsibility and fixed monetary values.

item.title: A Taxing Discussion
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: This article explores the historical origins of the U.S. income tax, specifically focusing on how World War II transformed it from a practice for the wealthy into a requirement for the general public. It examines the introduction of the 1040 form and the government's efforts to encourage compliance through propaganda.

item.title: Reading List 04/18/2026
item.description: This reading list covers a diverse range of topics, including advancements in quadruped welding robotics and the 'China Shock 2.0' economic phenomenon. It also explores emerging trends in transformer startups and recent anomalous movements observed in Chinese satellite technology.

item.title: Gaussian distributed weights for LLMs
item.description: This article discusses 4-bit floating point formats like NF4 and FP4 used for LLM weight quantization. It explores the relationship between these formats and the Gaussian distribution of model weights.

item.title: 4-bit floating point FP4
item.description: This post discusses the evolution of floating-point representation, tracing the transition from 32-bit and 64-bit standards to the current emergence of 4-bit (FP4) formats. It highlights how programming languages like C historically handled these sizes and sets the stage for understanding modern low-precision computing.

item.title: The electromechanical angle computer inside the B-52 bomber's star tracker
item.description: This article explores the technical inner workings of the B-52 bomber's 'Angle Computer,' an electromechanical analog system used for celestial navigation. It explains how the device physically models the celestial sphere to track stars and calculate precise headings without the use of digital computers.

item.title: Forgotten message from the past: LB_INIT­STORAGE
item.description: This post discusses the historical Windows message LB_INITSTORAGE, designed to preallocate memory for list boxes. It explains how this mechanism was intended to prevent the performance degradation associated with quadratic time complexity during item insertion.

item.title: Taking down my site on purpose:
item.description: The article explains the historical limitation of IPv4 addresses and the transition to IPv6. The author decides to disable IPv4 support on their website to encourage wider adoption of IPv6, despite the potential loss of accessibility for some users.

item.title: Pluralistic: Georgia's voting technology blunder (18 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow examines the historical failures of the electronic voting machine industry, tracing current issues back to flawed standardization efforts after the 2000 election. He explains how private companies colluded within the IEEE to codify their existing defective technology as the official standard to capture federal funding.

item.title: We Are All Playing Politics at Work
item.description: The article argues that workplace politics is unavoidable because humans are driven by emotions and incentives rather than raw facts. The author suggests that pretending to be above office politics only cedes control to others, as even seemingly objective fields like science are subject to human interpretation.

item.title: Adding a new content type to my blog-to-newsletter tool
item.description: Simon Willison demonstrates how he updated his blog-to-newsletter tool to include a new 'beats' content type. He shares the specific AI prompt used with Claude Code to automate the integration of this data from his Datasette instance into his newsletter workflow.

item.title: Join us at PyCon US 2026 in Long Beach - we have new AI and security tracks this year
item.description: PyCon US 2026 is scheduled for May 13-19 in Long Beach, featuring new specialized tracks for AI and Security. The post highlights the upcoming AI schedule, which includes sessions on AI-assisted maintenance, education, and running local language models.

item.title: Many anti-AI arguments are conservative arguments
item.description: The article explores the intersection between contemporary anti-AI sentiment and traditional conservative philosophical arguments. It suggests that skepticism toward artificial intelligence often mirrors long-standing debates regarding technological preservation and social order.

item.title: Here's What Agentic AI Can Do With Have I Been Pwned's APIs
item.description: Troy Hunt explores the practical integration of Agentic AI with the 'Have I Been Pwned' API. He balances skepticism regarding AI hype with a demonstration of how agents can perform genuinely useful security tasks.

item.title: The Mystery of Rennes-le-Château, Part 4: Non-Fiction Meets Fiction
item.description: This article examines the historical and pseudo-historical origins of the Rennes-le-Château mystery, focusing on the impact of the 1982 book 'The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail'. It traces how these narratives influenced the development of the video game 'Gabriel Knight 3'.

item.title: Book Review: How To Kill A Witch - A Guide For The Patriarchy by Claire Mitchell and Zoe Venditozzi ★★★⯪☆
item.description: This book review explores 'How To Kill A Witch,' which investigates the historical realities and societal motivations behind the Scottish Witch Trials. The author examines why women were targeted and discusses the lingering modern consequences of these historical persecutions.

item.title: Pluralistic: Tiktokification shall set us free (17 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow analyzes how Facebook’s shift toward algorithmic content, or 'Tiktokification,' prioritizes engagement over organic social connection. By forcing users to interact with strangers rather than friends, the platform seeks to maximize revenue at the expense of genuine user context.

item.title: datasette 1.0a28
item.description: Datasette 1.0a28 is a maintenance release that addresses compatibility issues and resource management bugs introduced in version 1.0a27. It introduces improved connection handling, new close methods, and an automatic pytest cleanup plugin to prevent file descriptor exhaustion.

item.title: SQLAlchemy 2 In Practice - Chapter 5 - Advanced Many-To-Many Relationships
item.description: This article serves as the fifth chapter of the 'SQLAlchemy 2 in Practice' book, focusing on advanced implementations of many-to-many relationships. It explores how to tweak standard relational database building blocks to achieve specific design goals.

item.title: The Power of Possibility
item.description: Anil Dash advocates for the Lower Eastside Girls Club, highlighting its effective community-focused model and successful outcomes in STEM, arts, and leadership programs. He encourages readers to support the organization through direct donations or by attending their 30th Anniversary Gala.

item.title: What I learned this week - Pretraining parallelisms, Can distillation be stopped, Mythos and the cybersecurity equilibrium, Pipeline RL, On why pretraining runs fails
item.description: This digest explores advanced AI engineering topics, including pretraining parallelization techniques and the mechanics of pipeline reinforcement learning. It further examines the challenges of pretraining stability and the evolving dynamics of cybersecurity in the age of AI.

item.title: Features everyone should steal from npmx
item.description: The article discusses the impact of npmx.dev, an alternative npm frontend that has revitalized development for the package registry. It highlights how npmx serves as a practical reference for registry features, including transitive install size tracking and security disclosures for install scripts.

item.title: I truly hate mostpeopleslop
item.description: This article explores the decline of social media writing quality, citing Joe Sugarman’s copywriting principle that the first sentence exists solely to hook the reader. It critiques the current trend of 'slop' content, where the focus on engagement has undermined the purpose of effective, compelling communication.

item.title: Newton diameters
item.description: The post defines Newton diameters, which are lines that intersect the zero set of an nth-degree polynomial exactly n times. It explores this mathematical concept using the example of a circle's diameter to illustrate how geometric lines relate to polynomial roots.

item.title: What’s up with window message 0x0091? We’re getting it with unexpected parameters
item.description: This post investigates an undocumented Windows message, 0x0091, which appears to be used internally by the system. The author warns against intercepting or relying on such system-reserved messages due to the risk of unexpected behavior.

item.title: RSS Club for WordPress
item.description: The author introduces 'RSS Club,' a method to create exclusive content hidden from website visitors but visible to RSS and Atom feed subscribers. The post outlines the technical requirements for WordPress users to implement this gatekeeping feature on their own blogs.

item.title: Why is it so hard to passively stalk my friends' locations?
item.description: The author explores the technical and social challenges of location-sharing tools, highlighting the tension between the desire for serendipitous social encounters and privacy concerns. He reflects on why modern technology makes it difficult to passively track friends' locations despite the potential for spontaneous meetups.

item.title: Pluralistic: A Pascal's Wager for AI Doomers (16 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow argues that focusing on hypothetical future AI existential risks is a distraction from the immediate dangers posed by unchecked corporate power and surveillance. He asserts that we should prioritize regulating current technologies used to exploit workers rather than speculating about AI's potential sentience.

item.title: AI cybersecurity is not proof of work
item.description: The author argues that AI-driven cybersecurity should not be viewed through the lens of 'proof of work,' where more computational power guarantees success. Instead, finding software vulnerabilities depends on model intelligence, as weaker models lack the reasoning capacity to identify complex bugs regardless of how much compute is applied.

item.title: llm-anthropic 0.25
item.description: The llm-anthropic 0.25 update introduces support for the claude-opus-4.7 model and new thinking process configurations. It also increases default token limits and removes obsolete beta headers for better compatibility.

item.title: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my laptop drew me a better pelican than Claude Opus 4.7
item.description: Simon Willison compares image generation capabilities between the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model running locally and Claude Opus 4.7. He uses his quirky 'pelican riding a bicycle' benchmark to evaluate the accuracy of the outputs, finding that the smaller local model outperformed the larger model.

item.title: datasette.io news preview
item.description: Simon Willison developed a custom preview tool to simplify editing the YAML-based news feed for the Datasette website. By leveraging Claude Artifacts, the tool provides a side-by-side view to validate YAML formatting and render the resulting Markdown content in real-time.

item.title: datasette-export-database 0.3a1
item.description: Datasette-export-database version 0.3a1 has been released. This update addresses a breaking change in Datasette 1.0a27 regarding the removal of the ds_csrftoken cookie, requiring an update to how the plugin handles signed URLs.

item.title: datasette 1.0a27
item.description: Datasette 1.0a27 introduces significant updates, including a move away from Django-style CSRF tokens in favor of modern browser headers. It also adds a RenameTableEvent for plugin compatibility and introduces new parameters for the Datasette client and database handling.

item.title: Speed is Not Conducive to Wisdom
item.description: The article critiques the modern obsession with speed, arguing that it prevents the deep reflection necessary for true wisdom. It posits that wisdom requires a slow, uncomfortable feedback loop of learning from failure and experience that urgency undermines.

item.title: zappa: an AI powered mitmproxy
item.description: The author introduces 'zappa,' an AI-powered mitmproxy plugin designed to intercept and transform web traffic to eliminate ads and intrusive elements. By using large language models to sanitize web content in real-time, the project aims to reclaim user attention from attention-economy business models.

item.title: Jensen Huang – TPU competition, why we should sell chips to China, & Nvidia’s supply chain moat
item.description: Jensen Huang discusses Nvidia's massive supply chain capabilities, asserting they can handle a trillion-dollar scale. He also addresses the strategic nuances of global competition and the rationale behind navigating chip trade policies with China.

item.title: A sufficiently comprehensive spec is not (necessarily) code
item.description: The article argues that a specification is fundamentally a set of possible implementations, whereas code is a single, specific implementation. While a sufficiently precise specification can be used to generate software, it remains conceptually distinct from code because a single spec can allow for multiple valid outcomes.

item.title: Pressed For Options
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: The author explores the challenges of finding reliable fingerprint authentication for Linux laptops compared to more mature Windows and macOS ecosystems. By experimenting with a budget-friendly USB reader from Temu, the article highlights the ongoing compatibility issues and lack of standardized support for biometric hardware on Linux.

item.title: The Tuesday Test
item.description: The author introduces the 'Tuesday Test' as a simple heuristic to determine if a package manager is truly declarative. A system passes the test if installing a package yields the same result regardless of when it is run, ensuring the process is isolated from hidden external inputs.

item.title: Why is there a long delay between a thread exiting and the Wait­For­Single­Object returning?
item.description: This article addresses a common developer confusion regarding delays when waiting for a thread to exit in Windows. It suggests that a perceived delay in WaitForSingleObject often indicates that the thread has not actually finished its execution yet.

item.title: Simdutf Can Now Be Used Without libc++ or libc++abi
item.description: Mitchell Hashimoto announces that the simdutf library can now be utilized without dependencies on libc++ or libc++abi. This change improves portability and reduces binary size for developers integrating the library into various systems. It simplifies the setup process by removing strict standard library requirements.

item.title: Pluralistic: Rights for robots (15 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This article explores the concept of 'corporate personhood' in the legal system, tracing its evolution from 19th-century judicial decisions to modern cases like Citizens United. It contrasts this with the 'Rights of Nature' movement, which seeks to grant legal standing to ecosystems to protect them from corporate influence.

item.title: Quoting John Gruber
item.description: Simon Willison quotes John Gruber on the declining quality of third-party software on Apple platforms. Gruber argues that the platform's competitive advantage is weakening as developers feel less motivated to build high-quality, native applications.

item.title: Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS
item.description: Google has introduced Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS, a new text-to-speech model accessible via the Gemini API. The model distinguishes itself by allowing users to influence speech output through detailed prompt engineering, including scene setting, vocal style, and accent instructions.

item.title: Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS
item.description: Simon Willison introduces a new tool that leverages Google's Gemini 3.1 Flash model for text-to-speech conversion. The post provides direct access to the experimental tool and links to further technical notes regarding the model's capabilities.

item.title: Quoting Kyle Kingsbury
item.description: The article discusses the emergence of 'meat shields'—human roles created to absorb accountability for the errors and failures of machine learning systems. It highlights how companies may utilize employees or third-party contractors to provide a veneer of human oversight or to act as scapegoats for automated system misbehavior.

item.title: datasette-ports 0.3
item.description: Datasette-ports 0.3 is a minor update to a utility tool used to monitor local Datasette instances. The new version adds visibility into the working directory and the full file paths of the databases for each active process.

item.title: Zig 0.16.0 release notes: "Juicy Main"
item.description: Zig 0.16.0 has been released with comprehensive updates, most notably the 'Juicy Main' feature. This update introduces dependency injection for the main() function, allowing developers to easily access essential resources like allocators, I/O, and environment variables via the process.Init parameter.

item.title: datasette PR #2689: Replace token-based CSRF with Sec-Fetch-Site header protection
item.description: Datasette has replaced its traditional token-based CSRF protection with the modern Sec-Fetch-Site header approach. This change simplifies templates by removing the need for hidden form fields and deprecates complex plugin hooks for skipping protection.

item.title: An Arm Mainboard for the Framework Laptop
item.description: Jeff Geerling tests an Arm-based Mainboard from MetaComputing for the Framework 13 laptop. This experiment demonstrates the modularity of the Framework chassis by successfully swapping between x86, RISC-V, and Arm architectures.

item.title: Nothing ever dies. It merely becomes embarrassing.
item.description: This article explores the 'Halo theory of science,' arguing that scientific ideas never truly disappear but instead persist in evolving, often awkward forms. The author examines how outdated concepts linger in our discourse, suggesting that cultural memory preserves them long after their original utility has faded.

item.title: Weekly Update 499
item.description: Troy Hunt shares his evolving perspective on using AI assistants like 'Bruce' for customer support. He argues that the value lies not just in full automation, but in how AI can assist humans in crafting responses efficiently.

item.title: Object Oriented Programming in Ada
item.description: This article explores the implementation of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) principles within the Ada programming language. It examines how Ada's unique features, such as packages and tagged types, facilitate robust software engineering and type safety.

item.title: Standing on the shoulders of Homebrew
item.description: The article critiques new Homebrew alternatives like zerobrew and nanobrew, arguing that their performance claims rely on skipping the complex, time-consuming tasks that Homebrew handles. By focusing only on simple package installation, these tools ignore the difficult parts of package management, such as Ruby DSL execution and post-install hooks.

item.title: Intersecting spheres and GPS
item.description: This article explains the geometric principles behind GPS positioning, specifically how distances from satellites are used to determine location. It details how the intersection of spheres creates circles that help narrow down a user's precise coordinate.

item.title: Finding a parabola through two points with given slopes
item.description: This article explores the mathematical process of finding a parabola defined by two points and their respective slopes at those points. The author investigates the geometric properties of 'Artzt parabolas' and demonstrates how to derive the general conic equation to solve for the specific parabola.

item.title: Why was there a red telephone at every receptionist desk?
item.description: This post clarifies the historical purpose of red telephones found at Microsoft receptionist desks. It dismisses the common myth that they were direct lines to leadership, explaining their actual function instead.

item.title: Pluralistic: In praise of (some) compartmentalization (14 Apr 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow explains his productivity strategy, noting that intense creative work and engaging conversations help him manage chronic pain by distracting his nervous system. He describes this as a form of beneficial compartmentalization that allows him to temporarily tune out physical discomfort.

item.title: Back button hijacking is going away
item.description: The article explains the deceptive practice of 'back button hijacking' used by platforms like LinkedIn to keep users engaged. By manipulating browser history through JavaScript, these sites prevent users from navigating away, forcing them onto the homepage feed instead.

item.title: Patch Tuesday, April 2026 Edition
item.description: Microsoft released a massive update addressing 167 security vulnerabilities, including critical zero-days in SharePoint and Windows Defender. Additionally, Google Chrome and Adobe Reader issued emergency patches for actively exploited flaws.

item.title: Trusted access for the next era of cyber defense
item.description: Simon Willison discusses OpenAI's new GPT-5.4-Cyber model and the expansion of their 'Trusted Access for Cyber' program. The post highlights the complexities of these cybersecurity-focused access tiers and compares them to similar initiatives from competitors like Anthropic.

item.title: Cybersecurity Looks Like Proof of Work Now
item.description: The article discusses how AI-driven cybersecurity is evolving into a 'proof of work' economic model, where system security depends on spending more tokens on exploit discovery than an attacker would spend to find them. This paradigm shift increases the value of shared open-source libraries, as the costs of securing them are distributed across all users.

item.title: A little tool to visualise MoE expert routing
item.description: The author created a visualization tool to observe how Mixture of Experts (MoE) models route tokens across different experts. The tool provides a transparent look into the internal decision-making processes of these complex neural network architectures.

item.title: give-them-two-choices
item.description: This article discusses the psychological strategy of offering two choices to influence behavior or decision-making. It likely explores how limiting options can simplify the process and increase the likelihood of a positive outcome.

item.title: That’s a Skill Issue
item.description: The author contrasts tech-centered and human-centered design philosophies, noting how the former blames users for 'skill issues' while the latter treats user confusion as a design failure. By highlighting the difference between demanding users master complex 'incantations' and designing intuitive systems, the post argues for a more empathetic approach to tool creation.
